title: Iran men’s soccer team makes schoolbag tribute in anthem as World Cup uncertainty remains
content:
Iran’s men’s soccer team returned to action on Friday for the first time since a military attack on the country from the U.S. and Israel, triggering wider conflict in the Middle East.

Iran is preparing for the World Cup, where each of its three group games — against New Zealand (June 15, at SoFi Stadium in Los Angeles), Belgium (June 21, also at SoFi) and Egypt (June 26, at Lumen Field in Seattle) — will be held in the U.S., with this month’s friendly games against Nigeria and Costa Rica in Turkey.

On Friday, Iran lost 2-1 to Nigeria in a match played without fans present in Belek, near Antalya.

Iran’s players wore black armbands and during the national anthem before the match they each held pink and purple schoolbags, which had ribbons attached.

An Iranian team ‌official is quoted by Reuters as saying the act was a symbolic protest over the killing of schoolgirls on the first day of the conflict.

An ongoing military investigation determined that the U.S. was responsible for a deadly Tomahawk missile strike on an Iranian elementary school on February 28. Iranian officials have said the death toll at the Shajareh Tayyebeh ​school was at least 175 people, most of them children.

Iran comfortably qualified for this summer’s World Cup, being held across the U.S., Canada and Mexico.

Amir Ghalenoei’s side clinched qualification in March 2025 after topping its qualification group, meaning the team has reached four successive World Cup finals and seven overall.

The nation’s participation in the tournament, however, has come under scrutiny. U.S. President Donald Trump has suggested Iran should withdraw from the tournament, while Iran’s sports minister, Ahmad Donyamali, also cast doubt on participation.

Donyamali told state TV earlier this month that the team “certainly” cannot participate in the tournament, “given that this corrupt (U.S.) regime has assassinated our leader”.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino said on March 11 that he had spoken with President Trump and received assurances that Iran would be welcome at the World Cup.

Less than 48 hours later, Trump later wrote on social media: “I really don’t believe it is appropriate (for Iran to) be there, for their own life and safety.”

Iran’s federation subsequently released a statement insisting “no one” can exclude them from the World Cup, insisting their participation at the tournament would not be determined by “any individual (or) country”.

Theoretically, Iran could boycott the tournament as a response to the U.S. attacks, but the side’s participation may also be taken out of its hands. This may be taken if the side’s participation is not deemed to be safe, or if the U.S. government decide to restrict Iran’s participation.

Global soccer governing body FIFA’s regulations give it broad discretion to call in a replacement national team or otherwise adjust the tournament — such as reducing Iran’s proposed group to three nations — accordingly.

Iran has said it is negotiating with FIFA to move its World Cup matches from the United States to Mexico, according to a post last week by the Iranian embassy in Mexico.

FIFA, however, says it has no intention of allowing the change.

Mehdi Taj, president of the Iranian Football Federation, is quoted as saying the body was “negotiating with FIFA to hold Iran’s matches in the World Cup in Mexico”.

Mexico’s president Claudia Sheinbaum told her daily news briefing that it is not a logistical issue for the country but simply a decision to be made by FIFA.

FIFA confirmed to The Athletic that it has been in touch with Iran, but stressed the fixtures are going ahead as originally announced in December.

Earlier this month, Iran’s women’s team competing in the Asian Cup in Australia, where they lost each of their three group games.

Iran’s team remained silent during the playing of its national anthem before their first game of the tournament against South Korea, leading to the players being labelled “wartime traitors” by an Iranian state television presenter.

Mohammad Reza Shahbazi said the players should be dealt with “severely” for “dishonour and lack of patriotism”.

Iran’s players did sing the anthem while saluting before their next two group games against Australia and the Philippines.

In the 2022 men’s World Cup, Iran’s players refused to sing the national anthem before their opening game against England, but did so in the following games against Wales and the United States. That tournament was played with the backdrop of widespread protests against Iran’s conservative clerical leadership.

Iran’s national anthem is tied to the 1979 Islamic revolution, which brought in a theocracy — a country ruled by religious leaders — which was headed by Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

The majority of the Iranian women’s football team who competed at this month’s tournament returned home last week. Seven members of the travelling party — six players and one member of support staff — had initially decided to claim humanitarian asylum in Australia, but five of them changed their mind and opted to return to Iran, including team captain Zahra Ghanbari.

Fatemeh Pasandideh and Atefeh Ramezanisadeh both remained in Australia, where they were pictured training with local club Brisbane Roar.

Sources with direct knowledge of events, speaking anonymously due to the sensitivities of the situation, told The Athletic that the players who chose to claim asylum came under intense pressure from the Iranian government, including having family members detained.

Iran’s club sides are also being impacted by the conflict. The last-16 stage of the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) Champions League, which includes Iranian side Tractor FC, have been relocated to Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.

The games were originally scheduled on a home-and-away basis in early March, but were postponed due to the conflict and relocated to Jeddah, where they will now be contested as single-leg games.

Tractor’s participation in their scheduled game against Shabab Al Ahli of Dubai has been put in doubt after, according to local media reports, Iran banned its sports team from competing in “hostile” nations.

Reuters cite reports from Iranian media that the government had banned sports teams from travelling to such nations over safety fears, which were said to specifically reference Tractor playing in Saudi Arabia.

“The presence of national and club teams in countries that are considered hostile and are unable to ensure the security of Iranian athletes and team members is prohibited until further notice,” the report cites Iran’s sports ministry as communicating. No reference was made to this summer’s World Cup.

The quarter-finals, semi-finals and final of the tournament will all be held on the same basis in the Saudi city.
